soc-01.title: The Sociological Imagination
explain: **Sociology** is the study of the relationships people form and of the institutions, groups, and norms that those relationships build up over time. It does not look at an individual's personality or mind. It looks at how the **society** around a person shapes that person's life. This department is a general-education course in basic theory, and every village, city, and figure that appears in it is a **fictional** case invented for explanation.

We usually think of hardship as a purely personal matter. When we lose a job, the first question is, 'Was I not good enough?' But what if a great many people face the same hardship? Individual effort and choices alone can hardly explain it, and we also have to look at social conditions such as the number of available jobs or changes in industry.

The ability to link personal experience with social structure is called the **sociological imagination**. The term was popularized by the American sociologist C. Wright Mills. He proposed distinguishing between two things.
- **Personal troubles**: difficulties that arise in one person's life or close surroundings and are explained by that person's character, choices, or relationships.
- **Public issues**: difficulties that many people share, caused by conditions beyond any individual's control, such as institutions or the structure of the economy.

The distinction is not black and white. In the same event, individual factors and social factors work **together**. How large each factor is gets weighed by checking how many people are in the same situation and how others in similar conditions are doing. That is why sociology does not stop at a single case and likes to use **rates and comparisons**.

explain.alt: Employment status in two fictional villages. Village Ga is shown as 20 circles for its 20 residents: 2 are filled orange (unemployed) and the other 18 are hollow with green outlines (working). Village Na has 9 of 20 circles filled (unemployed) and 11 hollow (working).

explain: The figure shows two fictional villages. Both have 20 residents, but the number of unemployed people differs. Hearing one person's story would not reveal that the two villages differ; the difference appears only when the rates are placed side by side.

examples.title: Re-examining one case through a sociological lens
body: Jiu, a fictional person, lost work when a factory in Village Na closed. At first Jiu thought, 'I should have prepared more.'

1. First, look at how many people are in the same situation. In Village Na, 9 of 20 people lost their jobs.
2. Next, look at a comparison. In Village Ga, it is 2 of 20.
3. Write down individual factors (preparation, choices) and structural factors (the factory closure, the number of jobs) separately.
The conclusion is neither 'Jiu bears no responsibility at all' nor 'it is entirely Jiu's fault.' The exercise in this lesson is to place both kinds of factors side by side and weigh the size of each.

soc-02.title: Socialization and Roles
explain: A newborn baby knows no language, no table manners, and no way to greet others. The process by which a person learns the language, values, and ways of behaving of the society they belong to, and so becomes a member of that society, is called **socialization**.

Socialization is divided into two kinds according to when it happens.
- **Primary socialization**: the process in early childhood in which a person learns speech, basic daily habits, and a sense of right and wrong, mainly from family and close people.
- **Secondary socialization**: the process in which a person learns the rules and expectations that fit a new position in wider groups such as school, a workplace, or a club. It continues throughout life.

The places that guide socialization are called **agents of socialization**, and they include the family, school, peer groups, and mass media. Socialization is not just one-way instilling. People accept what they learn, sometimes change it, and build their own way of doing things.

The place a person occupies in society is called a **status**. Statuses can be divided into two kinds.
- **Ascribed status**: a status given at birth or one that the person can hardly change. Examples: whose child one is, or which age group one belongs to.
- **Achieved status**: a status obtained through effort or choice. Examples: university student, club president, office worker.

Each status carries a set of behaviors that society expects of a person in that position, and this is a **role**. Since a person holds several statuses, they also play several roles at the same time. As a result, demands sometimes collide.
- **Role conflict**: a situation in which the demands of the roles of different statuses collide so that it is hard to do both.
- **Role strain**: a difficult situation in which there are conflicting demands within a single status.
Some textbooks use the two terms differently, so here we follow the distinction above.

The second: status club president, Sunday 10 a.m. event preparation. The third: status part-time employee, Saturday 2 p.m. shift.

body: Minseo, the fictional person in the figure, is a student, a club president, and a part-time employee. With three statuses, there are three roles.

On Saturday at 2 p.m., the supplementary class and the part-time shift overlap. The demands of two different statuses collide at the same time, so this is **role conflict**. By contrast, the event preparation on Sunday morning does not overlap in time with the other two roles.

On the other hand, if a club president receives both the expectation to 'treat members casually as a friend' and the expectation to 'make firm decisions as president,' this is **role strain**, in which the demands within one status conflict.

soc-03.title: Groups and Organizations
explain: A **social group** is two or more people who have relationships with one another and share, to some degree, a sense of 'we.' People who happen to ride the same bus at the same time are merely gathered together and can hardly be called a group. There must be a relationship of mutual influence for it to be a group.

Groups are divided into two kinds according to the nature of their relationships. The distinction comes from the term **primary group** used by the American sociologist Cooley.
- **Primary group**: a small group with frequent face-to-face contact, emotional closeness, and long-lasting relationships with people as whole persons. Examples: family, old friends.
- **Secondary group**: a group that gathers to achieve a specific purpose, where relationships are relatively contract- and role-centered. Examples: a company, a school, a political party.
In reality the two overlap. Even within a company, very close colleagues behave like a primary group.

explain.alt: Two panels. Group A has four people, and every pair of people is joined by a line, making six lines in all. Group B has seven people in a tree shape, one at the top, two in the middle, and four at the bottom, with lines joining only people at adjacent levels.

explain: In the figure, everyone in A is connected to everyone else, while B is a tree shape connected from top to bottom. When the number of people grows, a scheme that connects everyone directly makes connections increase sharply. If n people are all connected to one another, the number of connections is n × (n - 1) ÷ 2. This is one reason why a secondary group that has grown large runs on hierarchy and rules.

A large group intentionally created for a specific goal, with fixed roles and rules, is called an **organization**, and the representative way of running a large organization is **bureaucracy**. The German sociologist Weber set out the features of bureaucracy as an **ideal type**. An ideal type is not reality as it is but a model built by abstracting features.
- **Division of labor and specialization**: work is divided and assigned.
- **Hierarchy**: there is a structure of authority from top to bottom.
- **Rules and documents**: people work according to set rules and records.
- **Impersonal relations**: people are treated by job criteria, not by personal closeness.
- **Merit-based selection**: people are hired and promoted on qualifications and achievement.

Bureaucracy helps get work done in a predictable and fair way, but it also has drawbacks. The typical ones are **formalism**, in which the rules themselves become the goal, the hassle of drawn-out procedures, and **alienation**, in which people feel like cogs in a machine. Looking at both strengths and weaknesses is the attitude of this lesson.

examples.title: A fictional case: a neighborhood gathering and a city hall service desk
body: A gathering in which four friends from the village eat together every week has no particular rules or titles, and if one person is absent, everyone notices. It is close to a primary group.

The service desk of the fictional Hanul City Hall has a designated department for each type of document, application forms and processing order are fixed in writing, and everyone who comes is handled by the same standard. The features of bureaucracy show up well. In return, the drawback of formalism can appear, such as an application not being accepted if even one form is different.

soc-04.title: Inequality and Stratification
explain: In a society, valued things such as income, occupation, education, power, and prestige are not distributed equally to everyone. A state in which these differences persist systematically is called **social inequality**. Dividing people into upper and lower layers according to those differences is called **social stratification**, and each layer is a **stratum**. What criteria are used to divide the layers differs from study to study. This lesson uses only fictional societies.

The structure of strata is compared by drawing the population share of each stratum as a shape. Two typical forms are the **pyramid type**, with a thick bottom layer, and the **diamond type**, with the thickest middle layer. In the figure, Society Ga is close to the pyramid type and Society Na is close to the diamond type.

explain.alt: The stratum composition of two societies compared by bar width. Society Ga, from the top, is high 10%, middle 30%, low 60%, with bars getting wider toward the bottom. Society Na is high 10%, middle 60%, low 30%, with the middle bar the widest.

explain:
People moving up and down between strata is called **social mobility**.
- **Intergenerational mobility**: a difference between the statuses of parents and children.
- **Intragenerational mobility**: a change in a single person's own status over a lifetime.
- Moving up is upward mobility; moving down is downward mobility.
How easy mobility is determines whether we speak of a stratification system as open or closed.

Sociology has three broad perspectives on why inequality arises and what it means. Rather than one being the correct answer, they illuminate different things.
- **Functionalism**: sees society as a system of interlocking parts. It explains that some difference in rewards is needed to place suitable people in difficult work, but holds that excessive differences harm society as a whole.
- **Conflict theory**: sees society as a place where groups compete and clash over scarce resources. It explains that inequality is maintained as powerful groups make and uphold rules that favor them.
- **Interactionism**: focuses on the meanings people exchange in everyday encounters. It looks at how strata show up and become fixed through symbols such as speech style, clothing, and naming.

The three perspectives ask different questions. Functionalism asks, 'What role does this structure play in society?' Conflict theory asks, 'Who gains and who loses?' Interactionism asks, 'How do people understand and produce this?' Looking at one social phenomenon through all three gives a fuller picture.

examples.title: One phenomenon, three perspectives
body: Suppose that in a fictional society doctors earn more than people in other occupations.

- Functionalism can explain it as a reward system meant to draw people into work that requires long training.
- Conflict theory asks whether physicians' associations limit entry to protect their own share.
- Interactionism looks at how the title 'Doctor' and the respect it brings confirm status in everyday life.
The three questions are not mutually exclusive. A sociologist's job is to look at the evidence and weigh which explanation is more persuasive.

soc-05.title: Deviance and Social Control
explain: Every society has standards of behavior that its members are expected to follow. These are **norms**. Norms vary in strength and form. Typical ones are **folkways**, such as how to greet people, **morals**, concerning right and wrong, and **laws**, which the state enforces.

Behavior that departs from norms is called **deviance**. The important point is that deviance is not a property attached to the behavior itself; it **varies with which norms a given society has in a given era**. The same behavior may be ordinary or deviant depending on place and time.

In the fictional country of Haneui, laughing out loud in public places was once considered rude, but now it is nothing unusual. Even within the same society, laughing loudly at a funeral hall is deviant, but at an amusement park it is not. So to solve 'what is deviance?', one must first ask 'who sets which norms?'

All the methods by which a society gets its members to follow norms are called **social control**. It is divided by method.
- **Formal control**: control carried out by laws, rules, and public institutions through set procedures. Fines, disciplinary action, commendations.
- **Informal control**: control carried out in everyday life by family, neighbors, and peers. Praise, disapproving looks, ostracism.
Each has a **reward** for following the norm and a **sanction** for breaking it.

explain.alt: A four-cell table with formal control and informal control across the top and rewards and sanctions down the side. The cell for formal control rewards reads receiving a commendation; informal control rewards reads a neighbor's praise; formal control sanctions reads paying a fine and being disciplined; informal control sanctions reads disapproving looks and ostracism.

explain: The three perspectives also differ in how they see deviance. Functionalism holds that deviance can also be an occasion for society to confirm the boundaries of its norms. Conflict theory holds that the interests of powerful groups are reflected in the norms and influence who gets called a deviant. Interactionism looks at the process in which people's reactions attach the label of 'deviant' to some behavior and that label changes the behavior of the person concerned. This is called **labeling**.

examples.title: Same behavior, different definitions
body: Compare beating a drum loudly at night in two fictional villages. In Baram Village, beating drums every New Year's Eve is a tradition and is even encouraged. In Moraeh Village, there is a rule banning noise after 10 p.m., so the same behavior is subject to punishment.

The behavior is the same, but the norms differ, so it is not deviant in one place and deviant in the other. Also, if a person who breaks the rule in Moraeh Village is fined, that is formal control, and if neighbors frown, that is informal control.

soc-06.title: Reading Social Surveys
explain: Sociology does not talk about society in words alone; it checks society through **research**. Since survey results often turn up in news reports and other reports, we need an eye for reading numbers. This lesson also uses only fictional villages and fictional figures.

The entire target of a study is the **population**, and the part actually surveyed is the **sample**. To estimate the population from a sample, the sample must resemble the population. The basic method is to draw the sample **at random**, so that every member of the population has a chance of being chosen. If you collect surveys only in front of the library, too many library users come in and the results tilt to one side. This is called sample bias. Gathering only people who respond voluntarily also produces a bias in which only certain kinds of people respond.

**Survey questions** can change the answers. Common problems are as follows.
- **Leading question**: a question whose wording hints at which answer is desirable. 'Do you agree with this plan that everyone welcomed?'
- **Double-barreled question**: a question that asks two things in one item. 'Are you satisfied with transportation and housing?' It is hard to answer if you are satisfied with only one.
- Write neutrally, and make sure the answer choices neither overlap nor leave gaps.

explain.alt: Results table of a library use survey in a fictional village, with 200 randomly selected respondents. Ages 10-20s: 30 of 50 respondents used it, 60%. Ages 30-40s: 28 of 70, 40%. Ages 50 and over: 24 of 80, 30%. The question is, Have you used the library in the past month? Yes or No.

explain: When reading a table, distinguish **rates** from **frequencies**. The usage rate in the table is a value calculated within each age group. The overall usage rate is found by dividing the total number of users by the total number of respondents. We can speak of differences between age groups, but this survey alone cannot tell us 'why' they differ.

Two variables changing together is called **correlation**. If one goes up when the other goes up, it is a positive correlation. But a correlation does not mean that one is the **cause** of the other, because there may be a third factor affecting both.

explain.alt: A scatter plot of 8 months of records for a fictional seaside city. The horizontal axis is ice cream sales (boxes) from 0 to 120, and the vertical axis is the number of swimming accidents from 0 to 12. Eight points run from lower left to upper right, rising from about 1 accident at sales of 20 to about 10 accidents at 110.

explain: In the figure, the months with more ice cream sales also have more swimming accidents. But it is hard to say that ice cream causes the accidents. In hot months, more ice cream is sold and more people swim, so accidents can increase. Here temperature is the **third factor** affecting both.

examples.title: Rewriting a leading question
body: A fictional survey item: 'Almost no one opposes the plan to build another excellent library. Do you agree?'

This item makes agreement look like the right answer through its first sentence and steers responses to one side. It can be rewritten like this: 'What do you think about the plan to build another library? Choose from strongly support, support, oppose, strongly oppose, or not sure.'

soc-07.title: Marx: Mode of Production, Class, Surplus Value, and Alienation
explain: Inside the same factory, one person owns the factory and another sells their time for a wage. This difference is hard to explain by differences in character or effort alone. The 19th-century German thinker **Karl Marx** (1818-1883) placed the starting point for understanding society in **the way people make things** in order to live. The factories, wages, and hours in this lesson are all fictional data for explanation.

Marx called the way a society materially produces things its **mode of production**. A mode of production has two aspects. **Productive forces** are the capacity to produce, such as technology, tools, and labor power, and **relations of production** are the relations among people in terms of who owns the means of production (factories, land, machines) and who works. He held that the **superstructure**, such as law, politics, and ideas, is formed on this economic **base** and is influenced by it. However, later interpretations differ over whether to read this as the base determining everything one-sidedly or as the superstructure also acting back on it.

**Class** is divided not by the height of occupation or income but by **one's relation to the means of production**. Those who own the means of production and employ others are the **capitalist class** (the bourgeoisie), and those who have no means of production and must sell their labor power are the **working class** (the proletariat). Under this definition, even a high-earning professional employee is placed on the worker side if they lack the means of production, and a person who works in their own shop without employing anyone is placed in a position between the two classes.

At the center of Marx's analysis is the concept of **surplus value**. A worker works through a day, and part of that time is used to create value equal to their own wage (**necessary labor**), while the rest creates value beyond that, which goes to the owner (**surplus labor**). This remainder is surplus value, and the ratio of surplus labor to necessary labor in the working day is called the **rate of surplus value**. $$e = \frac{\text{잉여노동 시간}}{\text{필요노동 시간}}$$ The larger this ratio, the larger the share the owner takes for the same necessary labor. This is a calculation that has meaning within the theoretical framework of the labor theory of value, and that theory itself is still debated in economics.

explain.alt: A long horizontal bar represents a working day of 8 hours. The scale below runs from 0 to 8 at 1-hour intervals. The bar is divided in two at mark 3; the left section is labeled "Necessary labor" and the right section is labeled "Surplus labor."

explain: The figure divides an 8-hour working day in two, with a scale. Necessary labor runs from mark 0 to the boundary, and surplus labor runs from the boundary to 8. Reading the mark at the boundary in the figure tells you how many hours of necessary labor and how many hours of surplus labor there are. Even with the same 8 hours, if the boundary moves to the right the rate of surplus value falls, and if it moves to the left the rate rises.

Marx held that **alienation** arises from this structure. Summarizing the discussion in his early writings, the worker becomes distant from (1) the **product** they make (it becomes someone else's property), (2) the **activity of labor** itself (work becomes doing what one is told), (3) **human essence** as a creative being, and (4) **other people** (relations become ones of competition and calculation). The limitations are also clear. In modern society, middle positions such as managers, professionals, and small self-employed businesses are widespread, so it is hard to divide people simply into two classes. For that reason, class research today often takes Marx's viewpoint and revises it by subdividing the middle class.

examples.title: Calculating the rate of surplus value
body: Conditions (fictional): The working day at Saebit Bakery factory is 10 hours. Assume it takes a worker 4 hours to create value equal to their own wage.
Step 1: Necessary labor is 4 hours, and surplus labor is $10 - 4 = 6$ hours.

Interpretation: For every hour of necessary labor, 1.5 hours of surplus labor arise. If the time needed to create value equal to the wage falls to 3 hours (when productivity rises and the same wage value is created faster), surplus labor becomes 7 hours and $e = 7 \div 3 \approx 2.33$, so the ratio changes greatly even within the same working day.

Step 2: When interpreting, confirm that position, not income level, was the criterion. Even if Eunsu's income is higher than Hajun's, by Marx's criterion Eunsu is on the worker side.

soc-08.title: Durkheim: Social Facts, Two Types of Solidarity, Social Integration, and Anomie
explain: If Marx started from economic structure, the Frenchman **Émile Durkheim** (1858-1917) posed the question this way: what is the distinct object of study that sets sociology apart from psychology and philosophy? His answer was **social facts**. This lesson deals with concepts for reading group statistics and does not aim to explain or judge any individual's circumstances.

A **social fact** is a way of acting, thinking, and feeling that exists outside the individual and exercises external constraint over the individual. Think of language, the monetary system, etiquette, and law. They existed before the individual was born, and if one does not follow them, one meets reactions such as disadvantage or disapproving looks. Durkheim proposed observing such facts like things and treating them with statistics. This means that, instead of asking about each individual's intentions, we look at the regular patterns (for example, rates and averages) that society produces.

His answer to how society is held together is the theory of **solidarity**. **Mechanical solidarity** arises when members do similar work and share similar beliefs. The shared consciousness of the community (the **collective conscience**) is stronger than the individual, and sanctions that punish violations of norms are prominent. **Organic solidarity** arises when the division of labor has developed so that members do different work and need one another. Individual differences grow, but dependence creates solidarity, and sanctions are mainly of the kind that set wrongs right and restore the previous state. Durkheim held that as society grows larger and the division of labor increases, it shifts toward the latter.

explain.alt: Two boxes. In "Village Ga," six circles labeled "farmer" are grouped together with no lines. In "Village Na," six circles labeled farmer, baker, doctor, blacksmith, teacher, and merchant are joined to one another by many lines.

explain: In the figure, Village Ga has people doing the same work gathered together, while in Village Na people doing different work are joined to one another by lines. A line is read as meaning that one person's work needs another person's work. By looking at whether the members' work is the same or different and whether there are lines in the figure, you can judge which one is closer to which kind of solidarity.

Durkheim showed this framework in *Suicide* (1897). What he tried to explain was not individual motives but the fact that the **society-wide suicide rate** (a rate within a given population) differs among groups and stays similar from year to year. He sorted the types along two axes. When **social integration** (how strongly individuals are bound to a group) is too low, the egoistic type appears, and when it is too high, the altruistic type appears. When **social regulation** (how much norms moderate individual desires) suddenly collapses, **anomie** (normative confusion) appears, and when it is excessively strong, the fatalistic type appears. In this lesson you only need to understand the names of the types and the axes, and no specific cases are covered.

The limitations are also important. First, using group-level statistics to assert the reasons of individuals is the **ecological fallacy**. A high rate in a group does not mean a particular individual in that group is that way. Second, official statistics can vary with how things are recorded. Third, mechanical and organic solidarity are ideal types, so actual societies are a mixture of the two. Still, the view that explains social phenomena by the structure of the group rather than reducing them to individual psychology is still used today.

examples.title: Converting to rates for comparison
body: Conditions (fictional): Region Ga has 45 cases among a population of 300,000, and Region Na has 20 cases among a population of 80,000. By count alone, Region Ga has more.
Step 1: Convert to a rate per 100,000 people. Ga: $45 \div 300000 \times 100000 = 15$. Na: $20 \div 80000 \times 100000 = 25$.

Step 2: Compared by rate, Region Na is higher. Interpretation: social facts should be compared not by counts but by rates relative to population. Still, this alone does not settle the reasons for the difference between the two regions.

examples.title: Classifying types of solidarity
body: Conditions (fictional): Haneul, a remote island village, is made up entirely of fishers who observe the same ancestral rites and rules, and a person who breaks a rule is condemned in front of the villagers. Saerom, a port city, has hundreds of occupations and depends on one another's services, and contract disputes are resolved by having the party make good the loss.
Step 1: Haneul has similar work, shared beliefs, and punitive sanctions, so it leans toward mechanical solidarity.

Step 2: Saerom has division of labor, mutual dependence, and restitutive sanctions, so it leans toward organic solidarity. Interpretation: a given society need not be purely one type; we read how far the two types are mixed.

soc-09.title: Weber's Types of Action and Domination, and Goffman's Impression Management
explain: Marx put economic structure first, and Durkheim put facts about the group first. The German **Max Weber** (1864-1920) held that to understand society one must know the **meaning** people give to their own actions. This approach is called **interpretive sociology** (*verstehende Soziologie*). Half a century later, the Canadian-born American sociologist **Erving Goffman** (1922-1982) looked not at huge structures but at the staging of the moments when people face one another. This lesson ties these two viewpoints together as macro (structure) and micro (interaction).

Weber defined **social action** as action in which the meaning the actor gives it is directed toward other people, and divided it into four types by motive. **Instrumentally rational action** is action in which one sets a goal and calculates and chooses the most efficient means. **Value-rational action** is action that follows a value one believes in (duty, conviction) regardless of the result. **Affectual action** is action driven by emotions such as anger or joy. **Traditional action** is action following a custom long practiced. These are ideal types, so a single act may contain a mixture of two or more.

Weber also divided the grounds on which people obey commands, that is, the basis of **legitimate domination**, into three. **Traditional domination** rests on the authority of 'it has always been so' (hereditary kingship), **charismatic domination** on belief in the extraordinary qualities of a leader, and **legal (rational) domination** on belief in the legitimacy of law and procedure. As seen in Lesson 3 of Stage 1, the typical form of legal domination is **bureaucracy**. These types are also ideal types, so in a single government or organization several grounds are often mixed.

Goffman likened everyday encounters to theater (the **dramaturgical approach**). People engage in **impression management**, adjusting the image they show others, and where there is an audience they act in keeping with the role they have taken. The key is to distinguish the **front stage**, where the audience sees, from the **back stage**, where there is no audience and the performance can be relaxed. This does not mean the performance is 'false.' It is the observation that everyone chooses how to present themselves to suit the situation.

explain.alt: Two boxes. "Space A" lists "customers come in," "polite speech, neat clothing," and "menus, tables." "Space B" lists "customers do not come in," "jokes, grumbling, relaxed posture," and "ingredients, prep counter." An arrow at the upper left, "customer entrance," points to Space A, and between the two boxes there is a dotted passage, with the words "staff move between the two spaces" below.

explain: The figure is a simplified fictional restaurant. In Space A customers come in and speech and clothing are neat, while in Space B customers do not come in and staff use a relaxed posture and manner of speaking. Staff move between the two spaces. In this way, front stage and back stage can be separated by who can see within the scene (the audience's access). The same staff member changing behavior as they move between spaces is an example of impression management. In *Stigma* (1963), Goffman later also dealt with how the judgments society attaches to attributes different from the 'normal' are managed in encounters.

There are limits too. Weber's types are tools for organizing reality and do not tell us the actual proportions of behavior. Goffman's view looks closely at the moment of an encounter but does not separately explain larger frameworks such as ownership structure or institutions. So it is appropriate to read the three classical thinkers and Goffman not as competitors but as perspectives that illuminate the same society at different resolutions.

examples.title: Classifying types of action
body: Conditions (fictional): A student takes only the courses in which they score best in order to get a scholarship (Ga). The same student resolves not to cheat on exams even at a loss (Na). Every year on the same day, they visit family graves with their family (Da). When their favorite team loses, they get angry and shout (Ra).
Step 1: Ga is calculation of means toward a goal, so instrumentally rational. Na is a conviction independent of the result, so value-rational.
Step 2: Da is custom, so traditional; Ra is an outburst of emotion, so affectual. Interpretation: even one person's behavior shows different types depending on the scene.

soc-10.title: Bourdieu: Capital, Habitus, Field, and Distinction
explain: Even when people attend the same school and take the same exam, the starting line can feel different depending on family background. Income alone does not fully explain this difference. The French sociologist **Pierre Bourdieu** (1930-2002) held that inequality is passed on not only through money but also through less visible resources such as taste, manner of speaking, knowledge, and personal connections. The groups and scores in this lesson are all fictional.

Bourdieu broadened the economist's notion of 'capital' into four kinds. **Economic capital** is money and property, such as income and assets. **Cultural capital** is cultural resources such as level of education, knowledge, an eye for the arts, and academic credentials, and it takes three forms: embodied (manner of speaking, refinement), objectified (books, instruments), and institutionalized (degrees). **Social capital** is the benefit gained from a network of acquaintances. **Symbolic capital** is capital recognized by others, such as prestige or honor. One kind of capital can be converted to another to some degree.

**Habitus** is a system of durable dispositions embodied through long-term socialization. What one likes, how one speaks, and what one feels suits oneself come from these dispositions even without conscious thought. Since it is formed in the home and at school and guides later behavior, it can be called the way structure settles inside the individual's body. A **field** is a structured social space, such as school, the art world, or academia, in which people compete over a particular kind of capital, and each field has different capital and rules that count.

explain.alt: A horizontal bar chart. For each of three groups, Ga, Na, and Da, there is an economic capital bar (green) and a cultural capital bar (orange), and the horizontal axis has marks at 0, 5, and 10. Group Ga: economic capital 9, cultural capital 4. Group Na: economic capital 5, cultural capital 9. Group Da: economic capital 3, cultural capital 3.

explain: The figure shows the capital makeup of three fictional groups with two bars each. Bourdieu read social space in two ways. One is the **volume of capital** (the overall size, such as the sum of economic and cultural capital), and the other is the **composition of capital** (which of economic and cultural capital is relatively larger). His claim is that even if the volume is similar, a different composition shows up in different tastes and lifestyles. In the figure, you can read the bar lengths and add them to get the volume, and compare the two bars to judge the composition.

The representative study written with this framework is *Distinction* (1979). Bourdieu held that taste is not a neutral preference but a means of creating and confirming **distinction** between classes. This is because the very standard by which a taste is judged 'refined' comes from the culture of the dominant group. There is also continuing discussion that schools favor children from families with cultural capital close to this standard and thereby **reproduce** inequality. The point is that making evaluation look neutral is itself a device of reproduction.

There is much criticism of its limits. It is pointed out that habitus determines action too much and so has difficulty explaining change and individual choice, that conclusions drawn from data from one period in France cannot simply be transferred to other societies, and that it collides with studies of 'omnivorous' taste, in which class divisions of taste increasingly blend. Therefore Bourdieu's concepts are better used as a framework of questions about the paths by which inequality persists than as laws true of every society.

examples.title: Calculating volume and composition of capital
body: Conditions: the three groups in the figure. Economic capital and cultural capital are each scored out of 10.
Step 1: Find the volume. Ga is $9 + 4 = 13$, Na is $5 + 9 = 14$, Da is $3 + 3 = 6$.

Step 2: Find the share of cultural capital. Ga is $4 \div 13 \approx 0.31$, Na is $9 \div 14 \approx 0.64$, Da is $3 \div 6 = 0.5$. Interpretation: Ga and Na have a similar volume but opposite compositions, with Ga tilted toward economic capital and Na toward cultural capital.

examples.title: Reading habitus through a case
body: Conditions (fictional): Seoyeon grew up with reading books at home and visiting museums as part of daily life. In her university interview, Seoyeon was not nervous and spoke her mind naturally even on unfamiliar topics. Mingyu had the same ability but found such settings unfamiliar and felt awkward in the interview room.

Step 1: Rather than seeing the difference between the two as only a difference in individual ability, look at how well the dispositions they formed (habitus) fit the standards of the field (the interview format).

Step 2: Seoyeon's habitus fits well with the expectations of the field of the interview, and Mingyu's fits less well. Interpretation: even when an evaluation looks fair, the way of evaluating can work in favor of people familiar with particular cultural capital. This does not claim it happens in every case.

soc-11.title: Giddens: Structuration Theory and Reflexivity in Late Modernity
explain: Sociology has an old question. To understand human behavior, should we look first at individual intentions (agency), or first at the rules of society (structure)? Durkheim leaned toward structure, and Weber and Goffman toward agency. The Briton **Anthony Giddens** (born 1938) proposed that we not set the two against each other but see them as two aspects of one process. This is his **structuration theory**.

For Giddens, **structure** is not a frame hardened outside society but the **rules and resources** on which action depends. Because we know the rules of Korean grammar, we can speak sentences. At the same time, every time we speak a sentence, those rules are used and carried forward. This relation, in which structure **constrains and enables** action while action **repeatedly reproduces** structure, he called the **duality of structure**.

explain.alt: At the top is a box "Structure (rules and resources)" and at the bottom a box "Action (the everyday practices of actors)." Beside the arrow pointing from top to bottom is written "constrains and enables," and beside the arrow pointing from bottom to top is written "reproduces or changes through repetition."

explain: The figure shows this cycle. The arrow from top to bottom is the direction in which structure constrains and enables action, and the arrow from bottom to top is the direction in which action reproduces or changes structure. If rules are followed as they are, structure continues, and if people use the rules a little differently, structure also changes slowly. It is easy to understand if you think of how a newly coined word spreads and ends up in the dictionary.

Giddens did not see actors as beings dragged along by rules. People are **knowledgeable agents** who know a great deal about what they do. Within that knowledge, however, there is what can be put into words (discursive consciousness) and what is done in daily life without much thought (practical consciousness). Even if we cannot explain the rules of greeting, we follow them well every day.

In his later work he called modern society **late modernity** and stressed two features. The first is **disembedding**. Social relations are lifted out of the here-and-now encounter and extended across time and space. An example is trusting a bank and experts whose faces we do not know with our money and information. What makes this possible are **abstract systems**, namely symbolic tokens such as money and systems of expertise, and **trust** in them. The second is **reflexivity**. It means that it has become routine for people and institutions to keep checking and revising their own actions and rules in light of new information.

As a limitation, it is criticized that the duality of structure, being conceptually elegant, is hard to turn into concrete data analysis. The criterion for sorting out whether a given constraint is a constraint of structure or a choice of the actor is vague. For that reason, Giddens's theory is often read less as a tool for directly testing hypotheses in concrete research than as a frame of thought that helps us avoid debating structure and agency separately.

examples.title: Duality of structure: the case of money
body: Conditions (fictional): In Haneui, people accept paper certificates as money. Because there is a rule (structure) by which certificates pass as money, shopkeepers accept a certificate and hand over goods.

Step 1: Structure enables action. Because the rule exists, the act of exchanging a certificate for goods takes place easily. Structure also constrains action. If one uses a different certificate, the transaction is refused.

Step 2: People's daily act of using certificates reproduces that rule. If many people stop trusting the certificates, their behavior changes and the structure collapses too. Interpretation: structure does not persist by itself outside action; it is maintained by action.

examples.title: Trust and reflexivity in late modernity
body: Conditions (fictional): Jia checks her lifestyle habits by consulting the content of an online health information service whose people she has never met. The service revises its content each time new research appears.
Step 1: Jia's trust in the service is not trust in a relationship confirmed by meeting in person but trust in an abstract system, a system of expertise. This is disembedding.

Step 2: Each time the information changes, Jia and the service re-examine their own ways of doing things. This is reflexivity. Interpretation: this example is meant to show the theory's concepts and is not advice about which information or services to trust.

soc-12.title: Beck: Risk Society, Reflexive Modernization, and Individualization
explain: The big problem of industrial society was how to distribute scarce goods. But as by-products of modernization, such as factory emissions, large-scale accidents, and the misuse of information technology, emerged as new problems, the question changed. The German sociologist **Ulrich Beck** (1944-2015) set out this change as a theory in *Risk Society* in 1986. The cases in this lesson are all fictional and are not evaluations of any particular technology or event.

Beck held that whereas the **distribution of goods (wealth)** was central in industrial society, the **distribution of risks** becomes central in late modern society. Here, risks are things that science, technology, and industry produce and that individuals find hard to notice by their own senses alone. Their features are that the causes are invisible, the effects spread far and long, and they are hard to judge without relying on expert knowledge. Risks tend to spread across borders and classes, and Beck spoke of this as the **boomerang effect**, in which risk ultimately returns to those who produced it.

However, this does not mean that risks strike everyone equally. The likelihood of exposure to risk and the resources for coping may be distributed differently by region and stratum. It is appropriate to read Beck's argument not as saying that inequality of wealth disappears, but as saying that, alongside the distribution of wealth, the distribution of risk becomes a political issue. This leads to research that measures and compares the distribution of risk.

The key concept explaining this change is **reflexive modernization**. It means that the more successful modernization is, the more its side effects become noticeable, so that the principles of modernity (science, industry, progress) themselves become a problem and an object of examination. It resembles Giddens's reflexivity, but Beck particularly stresses how risk shakes trust in institutions and experts. He also speaks of **individualization**. As traditional frames such as class, family, and occupation weaken, individuals are required to choose their own lives and to manage the risks of the results themselves. It has two sides, in that freedom grows and burdens grow at the same time.

Another thing Beck pointed out is **organized irresponsibility**. Risk is produced by many institutions, experts, and agencies intertwined, so that no single party takes responsibility alone. A typical case is one in which each agency met its own standards yet harm arises overall. Consider a fictional sewage treatment case. The factory met its own discharge standard, the treatment plant its own treatment standard, and the local government its permit standard, yet pollution of the stream remains.

There are limitations and criticisms as well. Perception of risk is not always the same as the actual size of risk, and it is pointed out that it is hard to confirm empirically whether risk has really grown larger than before. As to the claim that risk crosses class lines, many research findings show that actual exposure is still distributed unequally. So the risk society thesis is better used as a framework that asks about the institutions that handle risk and about responsibility.

To sum up the three theorists in this unit, Bourdieu puts at the center how inequality is culturally **reproduced**, Giddens the process in which structure and action make each other and are **reflexive**, and Beck the **risks** produced by modernization and the problem of responsibility. They answer different questions, so rather than sorting one as right and another as wrong, it is better to hold them up in turn against the same social phenomenon.

examples.title: Comparing rates of risk exposure
body: Conditions (fictional): Of 1,000 residents of a village near a chemical complex, 160 reported respiratory symptoms. Of 2,000 residents of a village far from the complex, 80 reported them.
Step 1: Convert to rates. Nearby: $160 \div 1000 = 0.16$. Far: $80 \div 2000 = 0.04$.

Step 2: Compare by ratio. $0.16 \div 0.04 = 4$. Interpretation: the reporting rate in the nearby village is 4 times that of the far village. This gives grounds for forming the hypothesis that risk is distributed unequally by region, but the numbers alone cannot settle the cause (possibility of a third factor).

examples.title: Reading organized irresponsibility
body: Conditions (fictional): After a new synthetic material came into wide use, harm was reported. The manufacturer says it passed the statutory tests, the certification body says it judged by the submitted data, and the seller says there was certification.
Step 1: Note that each party claims to have met its own standard.

Step 2: That no party is clearly responsible for the overall result is the mark of organized irresponsibility. Interpretation: whether an individual party broke the rules and whether the institutional system as a whole prevents risk are different questions.

soc-13.title: Measuring Inequality: Quantile Ratio, Relative Poverty Rate, Lorenz Curve, and Gini Coefficient
explain: That two villages have the same average income does not mean the circumstances of their people are the same. In one village everyone may earn about the same, while in the other a few may take most of it. The average hides this difference. For that reason sociology and economics use separate measures of how income is **spread out**. They are tools for comparing in numbers the stratification structure seen in Stage 1. All figures in this lesson are fictional.

The simplest method is the **quantile**: line people up in order of income and divide them into groups of equal size. Dividing into 5 groups gives quintiles, and the income share of the top 20% divided by the share of the bottom 20% is called the **quintile share ratio (S80/S20)**. Another method takes the middle value as the standard. The income of the person right in the middle of the line is the **median income**, and using the proportion of people below half (50%) of the median income as the **relative poverty rate** is one of the internationally common definitions. The standard may differ by study and by country.

The picture that shows the whole distribution at a glance is the **Lorenz curve**. The horizontal axis shows the cumulative share of the population, accumulated from the lowest-income person, and the vertical axis shows the cumulative share of income those people hold; points are plotted and joined. If everyone's income is equal, the points lie on the diagonal joining the lower left and upper right (the **line of perfect equality**). The more unequal, the more the curve sags below the diagonal.

explain.alt: A graph with the cumulative share of population on the horizontal axis and the cumulative share of income on the vertical axis (both 0-100%). A dotted diagonal runs from the lower-left corner to the upper-right corner, and below it is a green curve that bows downward. Points on the curve: 5% at the bottom 20%, 15% at 40%, 30% at 60%, 55% at 80%, reaching 100% at 100%.

explain: Let us read the curve in the figure. The bottom 20% hold 5% of income, and the bottom 80% hold 55%. So the share of the top 20% is $100 - 55 = 45\%$. The value made using the area between this curve and the diagonal is the **Gini coefficient**. If the total area of the triangle under the diagonal is $A + B$ and the area between the curve and the diagonal is $A$, the Gini coefficient is given by the first formula below. A value of 0 means perfect equality, and the closer to 1, the more unequal. When there are only a few points, the area under the curve is approximated by adding up trapezoids. Since the horizontal spacing is 0.2 each, the second formula below applies, where y is the decimal form of the cumulative income share. $$G = \frac{A}{A + B} = 1 - 2 \times (\text{곡선 아래 면적})$$ 이다. 0이면 완전 평등, 1에 가까울수록 불평등이다. 점이 몇 개뿐일 때는 곡선 아래 면적을 사다리꼴로 더해 근사한다. 가로 간격이 0.2씩이므로 $$G \approx 1 - \sum 0.2 \times (y_{i-1} + y_i)$$ 이다($y$ is the decimal form of the cumulative income share).

These measures look at different things. The quintile share ratio looks only at the two ends and ignores the middle. The relative poverty rate only counts how many people are below the line and says nothing about how poor they are below it. The Gini coefficient summarizes the whole distribution in one number, but the same value can arise even when the shapes of the curves differ. A society in which the lower stratum has shrunk and a society in which the share is concentrated in a tiny top can have the same Gini coefficient.

There are more limitations. Income and wealth (assets) are different, and values differ before and after taxes and transfers are taken into account. Whether the data are at the household or individual level, and whether high incomes were missed in the survey, also affect the values. Also, such measures show **how much** inequality there is but do not say **why** it arises. Theories such as Marx's class, Weber's class, status, and party, and Bourdieu's capital are questions at a different level that ask for the reasons.

examples.title: Calculating the Gini coefficient from the figure
body: Conditions: the points in the figure. At the bottom 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100%, the cumulative income shares are 0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.55, and 1.00.

Step 2: $G = 1 - 0.62 = 0.38$. Interpretation: between perfect equality (0) and perfect inequality (1), this is slightly toward the equal side of the midpoint. The same method can be applied to other societies to compare them in numbers. However, since there are only 5 points, this is a value approximating the actual curve.

examples.title: Calculating the relative poverty rate
body: Conditions (fictional): The monthly incomes (in units of 10,000 won) of 10 households in a group are 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 200, 300, and 800.
Step 1: Find the median income. With 10 values, it is the average of the middle two, 120 and 140, which is $130$ (10,000 won). Half of it is $65$ (10,000 won).

Step 2: Count the households below 65 (10,000 won). They are 40 and 60, 2 households. The relative poverty rate is $2 \div 10 = 20\%$. Interpretation: the mean is $(40+60+80+100+120+140+160+200+300+800) \div 10 = 200$ (10,000 won), much larger, but the single 800 pulled the mean up. This is why median income is used instead of the mean.

soc-14.title: Social Mobility: Mobility Tables, Structural Mobility, Odds Ratios, and Status Attainment
explain: Knowing the stratification structure does not tell us whether a society is open. Even if the strata are distinct, it is an open society if people move freely up and down, and even if the strata look weak, it is a closed society if children stay in the same place as their parents. To see this difference, we must look at parents' positions and children's positions as pairs. The basic tool used for this is the **mobility table**. The tables in this lesson come from a fictional survey.

A mobility table puts the parents' (origin) stratum in the rows and the children's (destination) stratum in the columns, and writes the number of corresponding people in each cell. The **diagonal cells** running from upper left to lower right are the people who stayed in the same stratum as their parents (inheritance, non-mobility). Whether below the diagonal (moving to a higher stratum than the parents) is upward mobility and above it (moving to a lower stratum) is downward mobility depends on the direction in which the table is arranged, so first check the row and column labels. The figure is arranged in the order high, middle, low.

explain.alt: A 3×3 table with the parents' stratum (high, middle, low) as rows and the children's stratum (high, middle, low) as columns. Parents high: 60, 20, 20 (total 100). Parents middle: 40, 120, 40 (total 200). Parents low: 30, 100, 70 (total 200). The diagonal cells running from upper left to lower right are light green.

explain: There are two kinds of values read from the table. The **outflow rate** is the proportion, among those of the same origin (row), who went to each destination stratum (the row total is the denominator). The **inflow rate** is the proportion that each origin makes up within the same destination stratum (column); the column total is the denominator. Also, taking the grand total as the denominator gives the proportions of upward, downward, and inherited positions, that is, the **absolute mobility rate**. In the table in the figure, upward mobility is 40 people from middle to high, 30 from low to high, and 100 from low to middle.

The absolute mobility rate has a pitfall. When the **stratification structure itself changes**, for example when the parents' generation has many in the lower stratum and the children's generation has more in the middle and upper strata, upward mobility arises regardless of anyone's effort. This is called **structural mobility**. It can be seen by comparing the row totals and column totals of the table. The parents' generation is high 100, middle 200, low 200, but the children's generation is high 130, middle 240, low 130. Since the lower stratum shrank and the upper stratum grew, part of the upward mobility is the result of structural change. Mobility in which strata swap places even with the same structure is called **circulation mobility**.

So how do we measure a society's **openness** apart from structural change? The representative method is the **odds ratio**. Take only the two strata, high and low, and form a 2×2 table $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$. The ratio of the odds of ending high given a high origin, $a / b$, to the odds of ending high given a low origin, $c / d$, is $$\text{승산비} = \frac{a \times d}{b \times c}$$ A value of 1 means origin and destination are unrelated (perfectly open), and the larger it is, the more strongly origin predicts destination. This value is less affected when the row and column totals change, so it is good for comparing across societies or periods.

Another strand of social mobility research is the **status attainment model**. Blau and Duncan (1967) estimated statistically the paths by which parents' occupation and education lead to a person's own education, first job, and current job. A person's own education plays a large part in the middle, but the influence of parents did not disappear completely. It is a framework that measures the forces of achievement and ascription together. Limitations include that results vary with how strata are divided into high, middle, and low, that interpretation may change if one looks at households or couples, and that change cannot be known from the table at a single point in time.

examples.title: Calculating absolute mobility rates
body: Conditions: the table in the figure. A total of 500 pairs.
Step 1: Inheritance is the diagonal cells, $60 + 120 + 70 = 250$. Upward is $40 + 30 + 100 = 170$. Downward is $20 + 20 + 40 = 80$. The sum $250 + 170 + 80 = 500$ equals the total.

Step 2: Convert to proportions. Inheritance $250 \div 500 = 50\%$, upward $34\%$, downward $16\%$. Interpretation: half stayed in the same stratum, and upward mobility is a little over twice downward mobility. However, these are absolute proportions with the influence of structural mobility mixed in.

examples.title: Comparing two societies by odds ratio
body: Conditions (fictional): Society Ga's high-low 2×2 table is $(a,b,c,d) = (60,20,30,70)$, and Society Na's is $(a,b,c,d) = (40,30,30,40)$.
Step 1: Ga's odds ratio is $(60 \times 70) \div (20 \times 30) = 4200 \div 600 = 7$. Na's is $(40 \times 40) \div (30 \times 30) = 1600 \div 900 \approx 1.78$.

Step 2: Ga is 7, and Na is about 1.78. Interpretation: Society Na has a weaker association between origin and destination and is more open. The odds ratio has the advantage that it can be compared regardless of changes in the stratification structure, but since it uses only two strata, it does not reflect movement of the middle stratum.

soc-15.title: Economic and Organizational Networks: Weak Ties, Structural Holes, and Embeddedness
explain: Looking back at the routes by which we find a job or learn new information, an acquaintance we contact only now and then is sometimes more decisive than the close friends we meet every day. The American sociologist **Mark Granovetter** (born 1943) set this intuition out as theory in his 1973 paper "The Strength of Weak Ties." This lesson covers his argument and the basic measures of network analysis. The groups and figures in this lesson are all fictional.

A **network** is a structure made up of people (nodes) and the relationships (ties) among them. Granovetter saw the strength of a tie as a combination of elements such as the amount of time spent together, emotional closeness, mutual help, and duration of the relationship. Family and close friends are **strong ties**, and acquaintances at the level of a greeting are **weak ties**. Strong ties have many overlapping friends. My friends are likely to know one another as well, forming a closed group.

explain.alt: Eight circles, A to H. In Group 1 on the left, A, B, C, and D are all joined to one another by lines, and in Group 2 on the right, E, F, G, and H are also all joined to one another. The two groups are connected only by a single thick orange line joining D and E.

explain: The figure shows this structure. A to D in Group 1 form a tight cluster in which everyone is connected, and so do E to H in Group 2. The two clusters are connected only by the single tie joining D and E. A tie that joins different clusters like this is called a **bridge**. Within a cluster, everyone already knows the same news, so new information has trouble circulating. A bridge, by contrast, carries **new information** from a different cluster. This is why Granovetter said weak ties are in fact powerful. He did not say, however, that every weak tie is a bridge, only that a weak tie is more likely to be one.

There are network measures that can be used on the figure. **Density** is the number of actual ties divided by the number of possible ties. With $n$ people, the number of possible ties is $n(n-1)/2$, and $$\text{밀도} = \frac{\text{실제 연결 수}}{n(n-1)/2}$$ **Degree** is the number of ties a person has and is the simplest measure of **centrality**. In this figure, D and E have a degree of 4, more than the other nodes (3), but what matters more is that they stand on the only path joining the two clusters. This is called a position bridging a **structural hole**. The sociologist Ronald Burt (1992) held that a person who bridges the gap between groups that are not connected to each other gains advantages in information and control.

Another important argument of Granovetter's is the **embeddedness** of economic action (1985). Simple models in economics take the **undersocialized** view, seeing people as individuals who calculate regardless of social relations, and conversely there is the **oversocialized** view, in which culture and norms determine action entirely. Granovetter criticized both views and held that market transactions also take place through trust and expectations within the network of personal relations that already exists. As one example, merchants who have long traded with each other sometimes trade on trust even without a contract.

Limits and caveats are also needed. Weak ties are not always more advantageous. Emotional support and help in a crisis are provided much better by strong ties. In contexts such as job searching, the effect of networks also differs by industry, culture, and period. How the strength of a tie is defined and measured also differs from study to study. Therefore this theory should not be read as advice on how to find a job, but as an explanation that information flows along social structure.

examples.title: Calculating network density
body: Conditions: the 8 people in the figure. Groups 1 and 2 each have 4 people all joined to one another, and the two groups are joined by the single D-E tie.
Step 1: Number of actual ties. If 4 people are all connected, $4 \times 3 \div 2 = 6$. With two groups, $6 + 6 = 12$, and adding the bridge gives 13.

Step 2: The number of possible ties is $8 \times 7 \div 2 = 28$. Density is $13 \div 28 \approx 0.46$. Interpretation: within each group the density is a tight 1, but the overall density is only 0.46. A single overall average does not reveal this 'two-clump' structure.

examples.title: A bridge-removal experiment
body: Conditions: Suppose the D-E tie in the figure is cut.

Step 2: The pairs that can no longer reach each other are the combinations of the 4 people in Group 1 and the 4 people in Group 2, so $4 \times 4 = 16$ pairs. Interpretation: one tie is responsible for the connection of 16 pairs. In this way the flow of information in a network can be concentrated in a few bridges.

soc-16.title: Social Research Methods: Operationalization, Measurement, Reliability and Validity, and the Elaboration Model
explain: Concepts such as 'social isolation,' 'trust in neighbors,' and 'class consciousness' are easy to use in daily life, but it is unclear how to measure them. In Lesson 6 of Stage 1 you learned the basics of reading samples, survey questions, correlation, and third factors. This lesson goes a step further and covers how an abstract concept is turned into a measurable form, and the procedure for checking the relation between two variables with a third variable. All cases in this lesson are fictional.

The process of turning a concept into something measurable is **operationalization**. First, **conceptualization** fixes the meaning and scope of the concept (for example, trust in neighbors = the expectation that people in the same neighborhood will act in good faith). Next, an **operational definition** turns that concept into **indicators** that can actually be observed (for example, the degree of agreement on a 5-point scale with 'If I lost my wallet on the street, I think a neighbor would return it'). If a concept has several facets, indicators are sometimes set for each sub-dimension and combined. Which indicators were chosen determines how the results are interpreted, so the researcher must state them.

The nature of measured values is classified by **level of measurement**. The **nominal level** consists of categories with only labels (region of residence, type of occupation), and only same or different is judged. The **ordinal level** consists of categories with an order (satisfaction 1-5, stages of education), and we know greater and lesser but not that the intervals are equal. The **interval level** consists of numbers with equal intervals (temperature in Celsius), and addition and subtraction are meaningful. The **ratio level** consists of numbers with an absolute zero (income, age), and we can say how many times as large. The higher the level, the more statistical methods can be used.

Whether a measurement is good is judged by two criteria. **Reliability** is whether similar values come out when the same thing is measured repeatedly (consistency), and **validity** is whether the measurement is actually measuring the intended concept (accuracy). In the analogy of a bathroom scale, a scale that always reads 2 kg too high has high reliability but low validity. Conversely, if the values are erratic, reliability is low, so validity can hardly be expected either. Thus reliability is close to a necessary condition for validity, not a sufficient one.

Now for the method of checking relations. Suppose variable $X$ (the number of fire trucks dispatched) and $Y$ (fire damage) are correlated. The **elaboration model**, developed by Paul Lazarsfeld, **controls** for a third variable $Z$ (the size of the fire), that is, groups cases with the same value of $Z$ and looks again at the relation between $X$ and $Y$. The relation after control is interpreted in three cases. (1) **Spurious relation**: $Z$ is a cause that precedes both $X$ and $Y$, so when it is controlled the relation between $X$ and $Y$ disappears. (2) **Intervening (interpretation)**: $X$ acts through $Z$ to affect $Y$, so when it is controlled the relation shrinks or disappears, but the time order is $X \rightarrow Z \rightarrow Y$. (3) **Interaction (specification)**: depending on the value of $Z$, the size of the relation between $X$ and $Y$ differs.

explain.alt: A table of 200 fire incidents. The columns are many fire trucks dispatched and few fire trucks dispatched. All fires row: many dispatched had large damage in 68 cases (100 in total); few dispatched had large damage in 32 cases (100 in total). Large fires row: many dispatched 64 cases (80 in total); few dispatched 16 cases (20 in total). Small fires row: many dispatched 4 cases (20 in total); few dispatched 16 cases (80 in total).

explain: The figure divides 200 fires by number of fire trucks dispatched and size of damage. In the overall table, the share of large damage is higher on the side where many fire trucks were dispatched. But when we split by fire size, we can compare the proportions on the two sides. Here, the larger the fire, the more fire trucks are bound to be dispatched and the greater the damage, so size precedes both $X$ and $Y$. If the relation disappears after control, we suspect a spurious relation. The judgment, however, is made not only from numbers but from time order and theory. This is because even with the same numerical pattern, if $Z$ is a result of $X$, it is intervening.

Limitations: elaboration can control only the variables we have measured. If a third variable has been omitted, a spurious relation may be missed. If categories are split too finely, there are too few cases and the proportions become unstable. Also, this method is a procedure for **doubting or weakening** causation in observational data, not for proving it. Causal inference requires the support of research design (random assignment, time order) and theory.

Step 2: In large fires, many dispatched $64 \div 80 = 80\%$, few dispatched $16 \div 20 = 80\%$, a difference of 0. soc-17.title: Demographic Sociology: Demographic Transition, Total Fertility Rate, and Dependency Ratio
explain: A society's institutions are greatly affected by the number and age composition of the people who make it up. A society with many children faces larger issues about schools, and a society with many older people faces larger issues about pensions and care. **Demographic sociology** (demography) deals numerically with how births, deaths, and migration change a population. All figures in this lesson are fictional. The aim is to learn concepts and calculations through fictional numbers, not to forecast the population of any real country or evaluate its policy.

Let us start with the basic measures. The **crude birth rate** is the number of babies born per 1,000 population in a year, the **crude death rate** is the number of deaths per 1,000, and the difference between the two is the **rate of natural increase**. A population changes when the inflow and outflow of people (migration) are added to this. Written as a formula, $$\text{인구 변화} = \text{출생} - \text{사망} + \text{유입} - \text{유출}$$ (In words: population change equals births minus deaths plus inflow minus outflow.)

The framework that generalizes how these measures change over time is the **demographic transition model**. In Stage 1, birth and death rates are both high, so the population hardly grows. In Stage 2, hygiene, medical care, and food supply improve and the death rate falls first, while the birth rate stays high for a while, so the population grows rapidly. In Stage 3, factors such as education, urbanization, perceptions of the cost of raising children, and the spread of contraception interact, the birth rate falls, and growth slows. In Stage 4, both birth and death rates are low and population growth is gentle.

explain.alt: A graph of the demographic transition model. The horizontal axis is the passage of time, divided by dotted lines into Stage 1 through Stage 4. The solid orange line is the birth rate, and the dotted green line is the death rate. In Stage 1 both are high. In Stage 2, while the death rate falls sharply, the birth rate falls only a little. In Stage 3 the birth rate falls sharply, and in Stage 4 both are low.

explain: The two curves in the figure are a schematic. In Stages 1 and 4 the gap between the two curves is narrow, so natural increase is small, and in Stage 2, while the birth rate stays high the death rate falls greatly, so the gap widens. In Stage 3 the birth rate comes down to follow, and the gap narrows again. The gap between the two curves is read as a signal of whether the population is growing rapidly or not.

The level of births is summarized by the **total fertility rate** (TFR). It is the age-specific fertility rates (babies born per 1,000 women) added up over the 5-year age groups, multiplied by the group width of 5, and divided by 1,000. $$\text{TFR} = \frac{5 \times \sum (\text{연령별 출산율})}{1000}$$ This means the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if that year's age-specific fertility rates continued unchanged. The level at which a population maintains itself in the long run, allowing for mortality (the **replacement level**), is known to be roughly 2.1. Since it is a one-year value, it may differ from the number of children actually borne by a generation of women.

Age composition is viewed through the **population pyramid** or the **dependency ratio**. $$\text{총부양비} = \frac{\text{유소년(0~14세)} + \text{노년(65세 이상)}}{\text{생산연령(15~64세)}} \times 100$$ This is an approximation of the number of people that 100 people in the economically active age range must support. Using only the young as the numerator gives the youth dependency ratio, and using only the old gives the old-age dependency ratio. It is an indicator with many limitations, because not everyone aged 15 to 64 works, and not everyone aged 65 and over is supported.

The demographic transition model itself has limitations. It is a generalization drawn from early European experience, so other societies do not necessarily follow the same order and speed. It does not take into account movements such as immigration, and the theories explaining the phenomenon of birth rates falling below the replacement level after Stage 4 have not been reduced to one. We should also avoid attributing changes in the birth rate to a single factor.

examples.title: Calculating the total fertility rate
body: Conditions (fictional): Age-specific fertility rates per 1,000 women are 2 for ages 15-19, 30 for 20-24, 90 for 25-29, 100 for 30-34, 40 for 35-39, 8 for 40-44, and 0 for 45-49.

Step 2: $\text{TFR} = 5 \times 270 \div 1000 = 1.35$. Interpretation: if this year's age-specific fertility rates were maintained, a woman would have 1.35 children on average. This is lower than the replacement level of 2.1. However, it is a one-year value and not a prediction of the future.

examples.title: Calculating the dependency ratio
body: Conditions (fictional): A city's population is 180 people aged 0-14, 600 aged 15-64, and 120 aged 65 and over.
Step 1: The youth dependency ratio is $180 \div 600 \times 100 = 30$, and the old-age dependency ratio is $120 \div 600 \times 100 = 20$.

Step 2: The total dependency ratio is $= 30 + 20 = 50$. Interpretation: there are 50 dependents per 100 working-age people. Even with the same total dependency ratio, the institutions needed differ depending on whether the young or the old are more numerous.

soc-18.title: Urban Sociology: Urbanism, the Concentric Zone Model, Segregation Index, and Gentrification
explain: Even the same person feels differently living in a small village and in a big city. There are places where you know the face of every neighbor, and places where hundreds of thousands of people come and go and most are strangers. **Urban sociology** studies how the space of the city shapes and changes people's relationships and ways of life, and the distribution of groups. The cities and numbers in this lesson are fictional.

Let us start with the classic discussions. In *Community and Society* (1887), the German Tönnies distinguished the **Gemeinschaft (community)**, bound by feeling and tradition, from the **Gesellschaft (society)**, bound by calculation and contract. In "The Metropolis and Mental Life" (1903), Simmel held that the city offers too much stimulation, so that city dwellers come to adopt an attitude of emotional numbness toward people and events. In "Urbanism as a Way of Life" (1938), the American Louis Wirth defined the city as a space that is large, dense, and heterogeneous, and argued that these three elements increase loose, purposive **secondary relationships**.

The representative model explaining the spatial structure of the city is the **concentric zone model** presented by Ernest Burgess (1925) of the Chicago School. It holds that the city spreads from the center outward and forms several belt-shaped zones. In order from the center, they are the **central business district**, the **zone in transition** with many old buildings and immigrants, the working-class residential zone, the middle-class residential zone with better housing, and the outer **commuter zone**. Later, Hoyt's sector (wedge) model and Harris and Ullman's multiple nuclei model appeared and made up for what a single center and belts could not explain.

explain.alt: A city drawing made of four concentric circles. The innermost is Zone 1, and going outward are Zones 2, 3, and 4. On the right, the number of residents by zone is written. Zone 1 has 10 of Group A and 40 of Group B, Zone 2 has 20 A and 30 B, Zone 3 has 30 A and 20 B, and Zone 4 has 40 A and 10 B.

explain: The figure is a fictional city simplified into four concentric zones. The number of residents of two groups, A and B, is written for each zone. Urban studies looks at whether groups are evenly mixed in space from the viewpoint of **residential segregation**. A representative measure is the **index of dissimilarity (segregation index)** $D$. For each zone, find group A's share of the total and group B's share of the total, add up the absolute values of the differences, and take half. In the formula below, a_i and b_i are the populations of A and B in zone i, and A and B are the total populations. $$D = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \left| \frac{a_i}{A} - \frac{b_i}{B} \right|$$ 여기서 $a_i$, $b_i$는 구역 $i$의 A, B 인구, $A$, $B$는 전체 인구다. $D$ lies between 0 (perfectly evenly mixed) and 1 (completely segregated), and can be read as the proportion of one group that would have to move between zones for the groups to be evenly mixed.

Among changes in the city, a phenomenon of great controversy is **gentrification**. It refers to the process in which new shops and higher-income groups move into a relatively run-down area, land prices and rents rise, and existing residents and stores are pushed out. Assessments differ. Some hold that investment comes into the area, the environment improves, and jobs are created, while others criticize that long-time residents and small merchants lose their foothold. The actual effects differ by area and policy, so rather than presenting one side as the correct answer, we must set the positions side by side and weigh the evidence.

The limitations are also clear. The concentric zone model came from the experience of one city in the early 20th century and does not fit as it is the cities of today, in which automobiles, railways, and information and communication have developed. Against Wirth's theory, later studies (for example, those of Herbert Gans) raised the objection that close-knit neighborhood communities also exist within cities. The segregation index is also sensitive to how zones are drawn, so even for the same city, drawing the zone boundaries differently can give a different value.

body: Conditions: the four zones in the figure. A has 10, 20, 30, 40 by zone (total 100), and B has 40, 30, 20, 10 (total 100).

Step 2: The sum is $0.3 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.8$, and half is $D = 0.4$. Interpretation: it means 40% of Group A would have to move to mix evenly with B. This is the value when the city is divided by these zones, and it changes if the zones are divided differently.
